title: How do you build a safety induction?
seoTitle: How to build a safety induction
description: How to build a safety induction: what the law expects at the start of work, three content layers, delivery before exposure, understanding checks, records.
shortAnswer: Build a safety induction in three layers: organization wide content (safety policy, rights, how to report hazards and injuries, emergencies), site specific content (layout, site rules, hazards, emergency points), and task specific training for the person's first duties. Deliver it before the person is exposed to the hazards, in a language they understand, check understanding by questioning or demonstration, and record what was covered, by whom, and the result.
keyTakeaways: Several frameworks attach safety training to the start of work: the EU OSH Framework Directive on recruitment, Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act on hiring, and specific OSHA standards at initial assignment.
An induction is not one presentation. Separate what applies to everyone, what applies to this site, and what applies to this task.
Deliver before exposure. Task specific parts must be complete before the person does the task unsupervised.
Check understanding, do not collect signatures. Safe Work Australia says it is insufficient to hand over a procedure and ask for acknowledgment.
Visitors and contractors need a proportionate version; workers from outside undertakings must actually receive appropriate instructions under EU law.

sections.heading: What do safety laws require at the start of work?

blocks.text: Most safety laws require training suited to the work and its risks, and several name the start of employment or of a task as a point when it must be given. The table gives verified examples; it is not a complete list for any jurisdiction.

blocks.caption: Examples of requirements that attach safety training to the start of work
head: Framework
What it requires at the start
rows: EU OSH Framework Directive 89/391/EEC, Article 12(1) and (2)

Adequate safety and health training specific to the workstation or job on recruitment, on transfer or change of job, and on new equipment or technology; employers must ensure workers from outside undertakings have in fact received appropriate instructions
Japan, Industrial Safety and Health Act, Article 59(1)
Safety or health education for the work on hiring, and again under Article 59(2) when work content changes
United States, OSHA hazard communication, 29 CFR 1910.1200(h)(1)
Information and training on hazardous chemicals at the time of initial assignment and when a new chemical hazard is introduced
United States, OSHA emergency action plans, 29 CFR 1910.38(f)
Review the emergency action plan with each covered employee when the plan is developed or the employee is initially assigned to a job, when responsibilities change, and when the plan changes
United States, OSHA respiratory protection, 29 CFR 1910.134(k)(3)
Training before the employee is required to use a respirator
United States, OSHA construction, 29 CFR 1926.21(b)(2)
Instruct each employee in the recognition and avoidance of unsafe conditions applicable to their work environment
Australia, model WHS Regulations, regulation 316
General construction induction training for construction workers who have not completed it, or completed it more than two years earlier without construction work in the preceding two years

For detail see [EU OSH Framework Directive training](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), [Japan Industrial Safety and Health Act training](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training), [OSHA hazard communication training](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements) and [general construction induction (white card)](/regulations/general-construction-induction-white-card).

sections.heading: What should a safety induction include?

blocks.text: Structure it in three layers, delivered in order, so each person gets what applies to them and nothing important is buried in a long general session. The checklist below is an original template; its organization layer draws on the program awareness topics in OSHA's Recommended Practices for Safety and Health Programs ([OSHA](https://www.osha.gov/safety-management/education-training)).

blocks.caption: Safety induction content checklist by layer
head: Layer
Content
When
How understanding is checked
rows: 1. Organization

Safety policy and goals; how the safety program works; who to contact; how to report hazards, injuries, illnesses and near misses; workers' rights, including the right to report without retaliation; employer responsibilities; consultation arrangements and representatives
First day, before site access
Short questions; worker states how and to whom they would report
2. Site

Layout, restricted areas and traffic routes; site rules; main hazards and controls on this site; emergency procedures, alarms, assembly points, first aid and fire equipment; welfare facilities; personal protective equipment required on site
Before working on the site; again when moving to a new site
Walk through with the worker pointing out exits, alarms and assembly point
3. Task
Procedures for the first tasks; specific hazards (chemicals, machinery, energy, heights); required training under specific standards; equipment use; when to stop and ask
Before the task is done without supervision
Observed demonstration against the procedure; competency sign off

blocks.text: Where a task triggers a specific requirement, such as respirator use or hazardous chemicals, the task layer must meet that standard's content and timing, and its records must meet that standard's rules. Map these in your [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix).

sections.heading: What are the steps to build the induction?

blocks.text: There are seven steps, starting from the hazards and legal triggers rather than from existing slides.

items: **List the hazards and legal triggers** for each site and role from the risk register and the applicable standards.
**Assign each item to a layer** (organization, site, task) and to an owner who keeps it current.

**Write outcomes,** not topics: "Identifies the nearest exit and assembly point" rather than "Emergency procedures." See [writing measurable learning outcomes](/guides/how-to-write-measurable-learning-outcomes).
**Choose delivery per layer:** short facilitated session or module for the organization layer, a guided walk for the site layer, demonstration and coached practice for the task layer.
**Build the check for each outcome,** using questions, a walk through or an observed task.

**Set supervision rules** for the period before task sign off. Safe Work Australia's risk management code says high levels of supervision are necessary where inexperienced workers follow new procedures or carry out difficult and critical tasks.
**Design the record** and test the whole induction with a few new starters before rollout.

sections.heading: How do you confirm the induction worked?

blocks.text: Confirm understanding by questioning and demonstration, and record the result, not just attendance. Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on managing work health and safety risks (November 2026) says training should require workers to demonstrate competence, that "it is insufficient to simply give a worker the procedure and ask them to acknowledge that they understand and are able to perform it," and that training must be provided in a form all workers can understand ([Safe Work Australia](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-how-manage-work-health-and-safety-risks)).

In the United States, OSHA's policy is that training must be presented in a language and vocabulary the employee understands ([OSHA, April 28, 2010](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2010-04-28)). For multilingual workforces see [delivering compliance training in multiple languages](/guides/how-to-deliver-compliance-training-in-multiple-languages).

blocks.caption: Induction record template (original)
head: Field
Content
rows: Person
Name, role, employer (for contractors and agency workers), start date, language of delivery
Induction version
Version of each layer's content used
Layer 1 and 2 completion
Date, deliverer, result of understanding check
Task sign offs
Each task, procedure version, assessor, date, result, any conditions
Specific standard training
Items required by named standards, with the fields those standards require
Supervision status
Tasks the person may do alone, and those still supervised

sections.heading: How should contractors and visitors be inducted?

blocks.text: Give contractors the site and task layers, verified against their employer's general training, and give visitors a short, proportionate briefing. Article 12(2) of the EU OSH Framework Directive requires employers to ensure that workers from outside undertakings working in their establishment have in fact received appropriate instructions on the risks during their activities there. Safe Work Australia's risk management code notes that information and instruction may also need to be given to others who enter the workplace, such as customers or visitors.

items: Contractors: site layer in full, task layer for their work, and a check of licenses and prior training (see [training contractors and temporary workers](/guides/how-to-train-contractors-and-temporary-workers)).
Agency workers: agree with the agency who delivers which layer, and exchange records.
Visitors: emergency procedures, restricted areas, required protective equipment, and an escort rule where hazards warrant it.
Returning workers: refresh the site layer after long absences or site changes.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines induction content as concepts tied to hazards, sites and tasks, each with an assessment point, so the organization, site and task layers can be assembled per person and every sign off traces to a content version. See [onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles) and [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence).

faqs.q: How long should a safety induction take?
faqs.a: No general rule sets a length. It depends on the site, hazards and role: an office induction may take an hour, while a heavy industrial site may need a day plus supervised task training. Split it into layers so people are not kept in a long session covering hazards they will never meet.

faqs.q: Can a safety induction be done online?
faqs.a: The organization layer often can. The site layer works best as a guided walk, and the task layer needs demonstration and observed practice. An online module followed by a signature does not show the person can find the exit or operate equipment safely.

faqs.q: Does a construction white card replace site induction?
faqs.a: No. In Australia, general construction induction training under the model WHS Regulations covers general construction safety. Each site still needs its own site specific induction covering local hazards, rules and emergency arrangements.

faqs.q: When should an induction be repeated?
faqs.a: When the person changes job, site or equipment, when new technology or hazards are introduced, and after long absences. The EU OSH Framework Directive names transfer, change of job, and new equipment or technology as training points, and Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act requires education again when work content changes.

factCheck.claim: Directive 89/391/EEC Article 12(1): adequate training on recruitment, transfer or change of job, new or changed equipment, new technology; Article 12(2): outside workers have in fact received appropriate instructions.
Japan Industrial Safety and Health Act Article 59(1) and (2): safety or health education on hiring and on change of work content.
1910.1200(h)(1): training at initial assignment and when a new chemical hazard is introduced.
1910.38(f): review emergency action plan when developed or employee initially assigned, when responsibilities change, when plan changes.
1910.134(k)(3): training before requiring the employee to use a respirator.
1926.21(b)(2): instruct each employee in recognition and avoidance of unsafe conditions.

Model WHS Regulations regulation 316: general construction induction for workers who have not completed it or completed it more than two years earlier without construction work in the preceding two years.

Safe Work Australia risk code November 2026: demonstrate competence; insufficient to acknowledge procedure; form understood by all workers; information to visitors and customers; high supervision for inexperienced workers on new, difficult or critical tasks.

OSHA Recommended Practices action item 1 program awareness topics: policies, program functions, contacts, reporting hazards, injuries, illnesses and near misses, emergencies, employer responsibilities, workers' rights; right to report without retaliation.
